implementation_notes: The standard library's bounded channel is the pattern: let (tx, rx) = sync_channel(bound) makes SyncSender::send block while the buffer is full (try_send returns TrySendError::Full or ::Disconnected instead) and Receiver::recv block while empty, with recv_timeout for a bounded wait and rx.iter() draining until disconnect; a bound of 0 is a rendezvous channel. Dropping all senders disconnects the channel, so recv returns Err(RecvError) and iteration ends - the idiomatic termination signal needs no sentinel. std::sync::mpsc has exactly one Receiver, so several consumer threads must share it behind a Mutex (or use crossbeam-channel for true multi-consumer); send moves items into the queue, so ownership and borrow checking handle the hand-off the way other languages need discipline for.
pitfalls: std's mpsc supports only one Receiver; multiple consumers must serialize on a Mutex<Receiver> (the lock becomes the bottleneck) or use crossbeam-channel instead.
send() blocks the calling OS thread: inside an async runtime that starves the executor - use a runtime-native channel there, or spawn_blocking.
channel() (unbounded) removes backpressure entirely; choosing sync_channel is choosing the bound.
Drop order is observable: if the receiver goes first, sends fail with Disconnected and the producer must treat that as an expected shutdown, not a panic.

variants.name: crossbeam-channel (MPMC with select! and timeouts)
variants.idiom_name: crossbeam_channel::bounded(cap) with cloned Sender/Receiver and select!
variants.implementation_notes: crossbeam-channel is the multi-producer multi-consumer replacement for std's mpsc: bounded(cap) creates a bounded channel whose send blocks while full, Senders and Receivers clone freely so any number of threads can produce and consume the same queue, try_send/recv_timeout give non-blocking and bounded waits, and select! lets one consumer wait on several channels or a shutdown signal at once. Disconnection semantics match std's - when all senders or all receivers are dropped, operations return errors instead of blocking - which supplies the shutdown path. Reach for it when a single Receiver or all-or-nothing blocking is the limitation and an async runtime is not wanted.
pitfalls: recv() blocks with no timeout; use recv_timeout when the consumer must also observe a shutdown flag.
select! picks randomly among ready operations, so dispatch order is not deterministic.
Dropping all receivers disconnects the channel: send then returns Err(SendError) and the producer must treat that as shutdown.

variants.name: tokio::sync::mpsc (async, bounded)
variants.idiom_name: tokio::sync::mpsc::channel(capacity) with send().await / recv().await and close()
variants.implementation_notes: In async Rust the runtime provides the queue: tokio::sync::mpsc::channel(capacity) is bounded, Sender::send awaits while the buffer is full (backpressure without blocking a thread), try_send is the non-blocking form, and the single Receiver::recv awaits an item or None once all senders are dropped and the buffer drains. reserve() hands out a permit so a producer can hold a slot while preparing a value, blocking_send/blocking_recv bridge synchronous code (outside the runtime), and Receiver::close() starts a clean shutdown that lets already-buffered messages drain. Because it is single-consumer, spreading work across tasks needs a mutex around the receiver (which serializes it) or one channel per consumer.
pitfalls: The receiver is single-consumer; sharing it behind a Mutex serializes consumption and can stall the runtime if the lock is held across await.
A task that cannot make progress while holding a send permit can deadlock a cyclic pipeline - keep the stage graph acyclic and drain downstream.
Dropping the receiver makes sends fail; dropping all senders is the clean end-of-stream signal (recv returns None after the buffer drains).
